title: Who is wise? (Avot 4:1)
hook: Ben Zoma: the wise learn from everyone; the rich are content with their lot

segments.voice: Yesterday, ben chorin: the work isn't yours to finish, and you're not free to quit. Your line was don't finish, don't quit. Today, a skip ahead to chapter four.

The Talmud tells a story about a sage named Ben Zoma. One day he stood on a high step on the Temple Mount and looked down at the enormous crowds of pilgrims. Instead of being annoyed by all the people, he said a blessing. Think how hard the first human had to work for a piece of bread, he said. Plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding, kneading, baking. And I wake up, and all of it's been done for me, by all these people. That's the man who opens chapter four of Pirkei Avot, with four questions.
screen: `BEN ZOMA ON THE TEMPLE MOUNT.` → `ALL THESE PEOPLE.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Who is wise? Who is strong? Who is rich? Who is honored? Each answer flips what you'd expect. Today, two of them. Who is wise? Not the one with the most degrees. The one who learns from every person. Then a verse from the Psalms that, in its plain sense, sounds almost boastful. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have more understanding than all my teachers." But the Mishnah reads the Hebrew another way, which the words can bear: from all my teachers I gained understanding. Every person is a teacher. The toddler who asks why. The coworker you find difficult. The stranger who does a job you've never noticed. Everyone knows something you don't. Who is rich? Not the one with the most. The one who's happy with his portion, what he already has. Another psalm backs it up: when you eat the work of your own hands, you'll be happy, and it will be well with you. Now back to the Temple Mount. Ben Zoma looked at a huge crowd and saw bakers, farmers, weavers, all the people whose work fed and clothed him. He learned from everyone, and he was grateful for what he had. Wise and rich at once. Both begin in the same place: paying attention to the people around you, and to what you've already been given. Tomorrow, the other two questions.
screen: `FOUR QUESTIONS THAT FLIP.` · `WISE: LEARNS FROM EVERY PERSON.` · `A PSALM, READ ANOTHER WAY.` · `RICH: HAPPY WITH HIS PORTION.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Think of three people you'll likely see today, including one you don't especially like, and for each one ask: what does this person know that I don't? A skill, a kind of patience, a way of seeing; there's always something. Then, for a breath or two, notice something you already have that's enough.
Ben Zoma, the sage who asked who is wise. His answer: the one who learns from every person. And who is rich? The one who's happy with what he has.
Your line: learn from everyone. The crowd is full of teachers. That's two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Ben Zoma's four questions are often taught in Jewish classes, and 'who is rich? one who is happy with his portion' is a saying people quote about contentment.
